listenings.text: When I moved from Boston to London to run a project for a bank, I thought the language would be the easy part. It was the hardest. In my first month, I sent a plan to a senior director, and he replied, 'Very interesting. I'd bear one or two things in mind.' I was delighted. I thought he loved it. Two weeks later, I found out that he had asked my boss to replace the whole plan. My British colleagues were not being dishonest. They were being tactful, and they expected me to understand. The opposite happened too. My emails were short and friendly by American standards, but people in the office found them curt. One colleague told me, very kindly, that I came across as angry. So I made two changes. I started every email with one sentence that had nothing to do with the task. And whenever a British colleague said that something was quite good, I asked a follow-up question. It saved me a lot of trouble.

I've been writing letters to the other side in disputes for almost thirty years, and the most useful thing I've learned is to take the person out of the problem. If I write, 'Your client failed to pay,' the other lawyer has to defend his client, and the next letter is angrier than mine. If I write, 'There has been a failure to pay the March invoice,' the facts are exactly the same, but there is nobody to defend. The noun does the work. The same is true of requests. 'Send me the documents now' starts a fight. 'We would be grateful for delivery of the documents by Friday' gets the documents. Young lawyers sometimes think this is weakness. It isn't. The firmness is in the deadline and in what happens after it, not in the adjectives. My letters are polite to the last line, and the last line is usually the date on which we will file the claim.

reading.rtitle: What Your London Counterparty Really Means -- A Short Guide to British Business Email
paras: When Brazilian lawyers start working with a London firm, the first surprise is rarely the law. It is the email. A British partner who is unhappy with your draft will almost never say so directly. Instead, you may receive a note that calls the draft an interesting approach and lists a few small points to bear in mind. Read quickly, it sounds like praise. Read carefully, it is a request for a new draft.

The British habit is to take the person out of the problem. A New York lawyer might write, 'You missed the deadline.' A London lawyer is more likely to write, 'There has been a delay in the delivery of the documents.' Nobody is blamed, but everybody knows who was late. The same tactful style turns 'Please pay us' into 'We would be grateful for payment at your earliest convenience,' and 'You made a mistake' into 'This seems to be an oversight.'

Foreign readers often make two opposite errors. Some take every polite phrase literally and wait for weeks, when in fact they have already been chased twice. Others reply in a style so direct that it comes across as curt. A one-line answer such as 'No. Clause 9 is not negotiable.' may be perfectly clear in São Paulo, but in London it can sound almost aggressive. It is usually wiser to err on the side of caution and add one sentence of context.

There is also a code worth learning. With all due respect usually means that the writer disagrees completely. A gentle reminder means that the writer is already annoyed. Regrettably, we are unable to agree is a firm no. None of this makes British email dishonest. It is simply a different way of being polite, and the reader is expected to do some of the work. The good news is that the code can be learned, and that a little toning down of your own style will make the other side far more willing to help.
